The Tourne Expre Is a Slovenian-Built Camper Van With a Patended Bed System and a Premium Interior
26 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Camerpvans
Meet the Tourne Expre, a camper van based on a Fiat Ducato L3. It was created by Tourne Campervans, a Pivka, Slovenia-based company specializing in journey-ready, hand-assembled camper vans.
As always, let's first take a look at the outside. This van doesn't have that many elements that hint at its "camper DNA" – it has more of a simple exterior setup, at least when compared to other mobile homes.
The vehicle rides on black 16-inch Ducato alloy wheels wrapped in all-season tires. On top of the rig, you'll come across a Thule Omnistor manual awning and a 140 W solar panel.
Other notable exterior mods are a gas adapter, a water hookup, a compartment that houses an outdoor shower, and two windows on the sides. Moreover, a Thule Slide Out electric entry step will make it easier for you to enter.
The van's inside is a lot more interesting than the exterior. A roomy, cleverly arranged interior will welcome you. Tourne Campervans is all about high quality when it comes to designing interiors.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Camerpvans For instance, the company makes all the furniture in-house. Moreover, it uses a compact material pressed very hard together mixed with resin to create the countertops and tabletops.
You'll notice poplar plywood cabinetry – poplar plywood is quite popular among camper van builders due to how lightweight it is.
The plywood is then covered with HPL (high pressure laminate) to make it waterproof, and the edges are sealed with ABS tape. This process makes for a light yet solid setup. The rest of the design in this van consists of blue marine-grade flooring and cream-colored wall panels.
The interior has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. What's more, the driver and passenger seats, proudly branded with "Tourne," are mounted on swivel bases.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Camerpvans That means you can turn them around and create a seating area out of the cabin after you've parked somewhere. This front seating area continues straight ahead of the entrance in the form of a massive table and a dual bench seat complete with seatbelts.
So, four people can be comfortably accommodated in the front part of the van. Furthermore, above, you'll come across a large overhead cabinet.
One of the van's highlights is Tourne's patented Dream4 system, which allows you to turn the bench and table into a bed that can sleep two kids, or even two adults if they don't mind a snug fit.
To set it up, you must use the tabletop and several other panels to create a platform which also has slide-out parts. Then, rearrange the cushions and pull out one of the drawers in the kitchen.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Camerpvans Next, we have the kitchen on the passenger side. It features a two-burner stovetop with a cover, a sink with a folding faucet, a tall 78-liter fridge with a freezer compartment, and a flip-up table for additional counter space.
A pull-out pantry, an overhead cabinet, a spice rack, and two large drawers with multiple compartments are available for storage.
On the opposite side, Tourne Campervans installed a facility that most people prefer having when traveling by camper van: a bathroom. It boasts a swiveling toilet, a cabinet with a mirror, and a sink with a pull-out sprayer that doubles as a showerhead.
The final part of the living space is the bedroom in the rear. There's definitely enough room for two people to be comfortably accommodated here thanks to the large bed – to be specific, it measures 190 centimeters (74 inches) in length and 140 centimeters (55 inches) in width.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Camerpvans Two large panels make up the bed platform. They are attached to hinges and can be lifted up and secured upright. That creates a lot of room to haul large items and lets you step inside the van through the back door and have a hallway spanning the entire length of the van.
The bedroom also offers two overhead cabinets with shelves under them, charging points, an awning-style window on the driver's side, and a large skylight above that can be opened.
Finally, the space underneath the bedroom was turned into a garage. It offers a decent amount of room for storage and has two boxes on the sides that accommodate part of the utility systems.
Usually, the power system inside a camper van is housed in the garage or at least in the rear part of the van. Things are different inside this rig – the builders installed a 100 Ah battery underneath the passenger seat, and some of the other components in other spots, like in the base of the double bench seat.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Camerpvans Three charging sources are available: solar power, shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a 90-liter (23-gallon) freshwater tank, an insulated and heated greywater tank mounted underneath the vehicle, and an outdoor shower. The greywater tank has an electric dump valve, so it can be dumped at the flip of a switch.
The last important utility system in this van is a Webasto air heater. It even has a vent that goes in the bathroom so you can pre-heat it before stepping in for a shower - that also means you can use the bathroom as a drying area. After you're done showering, you can open the skylight integrated into the bathroom's ceiling to let the moisture out.
The thermostat for the heater is conveniently located above the van's sliding door, next to a display that lets you monitor the power and water systems.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Camerpvans All in all, the Tourne Expre is a premium home on wheels that's fully equipped and ready for the road. There's one more decisive aspect to mention: pricing.
The Tourne Expre is available starting at €74,725 ($83,652), and it includes everything I presented above, as well as the base vehicle. Extras include a bed step for easy access, a Thule bike rack, and a Truma Combi heater. The conversion itself in its base form costs €13,580 ($15,177) - that's an excellent deal considering what you're getting.

Hyundai reveals new IONIQ 6 prices and range in the UK
Hyundai opened orders for the all-new IONIQ 6 in the UK, starting at £33,240 ($45,000), including the Electric Car Grant (ECG).
The “evolved” electrified streamliner brings a sharp new design, a refined interior, and a bigger battery for longer range.

It includes Hyundai’s new infotainment setup, including dual 12.3″ navigation and infotainment screens with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto capabilities.

Other added features included with the N-Line Evo trim include Surround View Monitor, Remote Smart Parking Assist, Parking Collision Avoidance Assist, Digital Key 2, Walk-Away Lock, exterior Vehicle-to-Load adaptor, and BOSE premium audio.
Both the IONIQ 6 N-Line and N-Line Evo use the 84 kWh battery, providing up to 364 miles of driving range in RWD and up to 354 miles with the AWD powertrain.

Postal operators in Norway and Germany are adding significant parcel capacity and making operational adjustments to handle an expected flood of packages and gift cards in the weeks leading up to Christmas.
Posten Bring, the state-owned postal services and logistics provider in Norway, has installed hundreds more parcel lockers to offer more flexible delivery options and recently opened its largest parcel distribution center.
Norway Post has established new locations and upgraded the size of 300 existing parcel lockers this year in anticipation of record parcel volumes during the holiday shipping season, the company said in a news release on Friday. Posten Bring operates two brands: Posten for the private market within Norway and Bring for the business market and cross-border e-commerce shipments.
The number of parcels delivered to parcel lockers in Norway in August broke last year’s Christmas record, indicating that demand for parcel boxes will be even greater this Christmas season, Norway Post said. From January to September, the number of parcels delivered to so-called Pakkeboks increased by around 50% compared to the same period last year.
Posten Bring encourages consumers to pick up packages as quickly as possible during the busy season because it frees up units for replenishment when millions of packages are due to arrive in a short time. At popular locations, Posten will replenish with new packages several times a day. More than nine out of 10 packages are collected within four days. On average, it takes about 26.5 hours for packages to be collected.
Earlier this month, Posten Bring opened its largest parcel terminal, capable of handling more than 500,000 packages per day.
The automated sort facility is located in Moss, five minutes from a major highway, and will mainly handle import volumes from Sweden and Denmark, in addition to local packages from Østfold. During heavy volume peaks, the terminal will also relieve Posten Bring’s logistics center in Oslo, the country’s main terminal for parcel sorting.
The postal carrier said the facility has plenty of room to accommodate future growth.
Deutsche Post
In Germany, DHL’s Post & Parcel division, doing business as Deutsche Post, said Friday it will increase capacity for processing and delivering letters and parcels, hire additional temporary staff and continue to expand its network of parcel stations. Planning for the Christmas season has been going on for months.
( Photo: DHL Post & Parcel Germany)
The postal operator plans to add more than 500 more parcel lockers nationwide by the end of the year. It will also hire more than 10,000 temporary workers this year to support its more-than 150,000 employees making deliveries and working in mail and parcel centers. Post & Parcel Germany has also created additional capacity at its sorting facilities to handle the increasing volume of mail, is planning about 9,500 separate delivery routes for the busiest weeks and will again deploy about 11,000 extra vehicles to ensure it can reliably sort, transport and deliver millions of letters and parcels during the holiday rush, it said in a news release.
“Flexibility is very important to many customers today. That’s why parcel lockers have become an integral part of everyday parcel delivery. They enable the sending and receiving of parcels regardless of opening hours and at the same time help us to efficiently manage increasing parcel volumes. This is a great advantage, especially in the run-up to Christmas,” said Nikola Hagleitner, a Post & Parcel Germany board member.
For sending and receiving parcels, customers across Germany now have access to about 19,500 DHL Packstations (automated, self-service locker systems that allow users to send, receive and drop-off parcels around the clock), Poststations (digital Deutsche Post retail outlets where users can take care of postal business), and partner-operated DeinFach automated parcel lockers.
The U.S. Postal Service recently outlined the ways it has prepared for the upcoming peak season and also said it was hiring 10,000 temporary workers.

Arkansas Highway Police and federal law enforcement agencies conducted a sweeping 48-hour commercial vehicle enforcement operation that resulted in 183 English-language proficiency violations, 44 criminal arrests and more than 1,000 motor carrier safety violations.
The crackdown, dubbed Operation Highway Shield , took place from 6 a.m. Tuesday through 6 a.m. Thursday (Oct. 27-29), targeting unsafe commercial vehicles, unqualified truck drivers and criminal activity along Arkansas highways.
According to the Arkansas Department of Transportation, officers conducted 1,724 Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration inspections, placing 393 drivers and commercial motor vehicles out of service .
Authorities also identified more than 330 unqualified or unauthorized drivers and reported 74 immigration violations that resulted in federal immigration enforcement.
Arkansas enforcement operation by the numbers
Enforcement category | Results
Commercial vehicle inspections | 1,724
Drivers and vehicles placed out of service | 393
Unqualified or unauthorized drivers identified | More than 330
English-language proficiency disqualifications | 183
Immigration violations resulting in federal enforcement | 74
Motor carrier safety violations | More than 1,000
Criminal arrests | 44
Traffic citations and warnings | 369
Stolen trailers recovered | 1
Source: Arkansas Department of Transportation , Oct. 29, 2026.
During the two-day enforcement campaign, Arkansas Highway Police conducted enhanced inspections at designated weigh stations along interstate highways and other approved commercial vehicle corridors.
The operation focused on identifying unqualified drivers, unsafe vehicles, fraudulent trucking practices and criminal activity.
Officers also investigated suspected drug trafficking, human trafficking and smuggling, cargo theft, and stolen commercial vehicles and trailers encountered during inspections.
Authorities recovered one stolen trailer, although officials did not disclose its value or provide details about the circumstances surrounding the theft.
The state also did not provide a breakdown of the criminal arrests, the specific violations behind the out-of-service orders or the immigration enforcement outcomes.
The Arkansas enforcement campaign follows two previous waves of Operation Highway Shield conducted earlier this year.
The first operation took place in Florida in March, when inspectors conducted more than 3,300 inspections and placed 176 drivers out of service, including 54 for English-language proficiency deficiencies.
Florida authorities also made 35 criminal-related arrests and took 42 individuals into custody for violations of federal immigration laws.
A second enforcement wave, conducted July 28-30 across Illinois, Indiana, Iowa and Ohio, resulted in 766 drivers and vehicles being placed out of service.
Federal officials reported 86 arrests, 51 immigration detentions and 36 English-language proficiency violations during the Midwest operation.
Authorities also recovered nearly $1 million in stolen cargo.
Why it matters: The results highlight expanding federal-state enforcement targeting driver qualifications, trucking safety and criminal activity along major freight corridors.

Remember Little Hoss, the Unbeaten Dual-Quad 1967 Camaro Z/28 Drag Champion That Spawned the ZL1
87 photos
Photo: Facebook/Ryan Snyder
Imagine side-stepping the clutch at 6,000 rpm while a solid-lifter small-block V8 screams past 8,500 rpm down a Midwestern dragstrip. Before the legendary aluminum-block ZL1 ever terrorized quarter-mile asphalt, one 1967 Chevrolet Camaro Z/28 put rural La Harpe, Illinois, on the high-performance map. Known simply as “Little Hoss,” this giant-slaying pony car won 65 out of 68 races and shattered 11 national records across two unforgettable seasons of stock-class warfare.
Today, Little Hoss sits in the private stable of Bradenton, Florida collector Ryan Snyder, who recently showcased the historic machine alongside automotive journalist Jim Campisano on the Muscle Car Campy YouTube channel.
White hand-lettered livery announces “302 CU. IN.” on the front fenders, “Little Hoss” on the doors, “FRED GIBB CHEVROLET LA HARPE” along the rear quarters, and “Herb Fox” above the wide rear Goodyear racing slicks. Up front, 15-inch silver steel rally wheels without trim rings or caps wear redline bias-ply tires, while the black vinyl cabin shows a 5,759-mile (9,268-kilometer) odometer reading.
Inside that sparse cockpit, a dash-mounted tachometer, two under-dash auxiliary gauges, and a floor-mounted 4-speed manual shifter are just about all the driver got back in 1967. When Chevrolet introduced the Camaro for 1967 across its Norwood, Ohio, and Van Nuys, California plants, total production reached 220,906 units, comprising 160,648 coupes and 25,141 convertibles alongside 64,842 Rally Sport packages, 34,411 Super Sport models, and 104 Pace Car replicas.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Yet the lineup lacked a dedicated road racer, one that would really bring the heat hard down on Carroll Shelby’s Mustangs. To homologate the Camaro for the Sports Car Club of America Trans-American Sedan Championship, Product Promotion Engineering manager Vince Piggins created Regular Production Option Z28 in December 1966.
Because Trans-Am rules limited engine displacement to 305 cubic inches (5.0 liters), Chevrolet engineers mated a forged-steel 283-cubic-inch (4.6-liter) crankshaft featuring a 3.00-inch stroke with a 327-cubic-inch (5.4-liter) block featuring a 4.00-inch bore to arrive at the sweet-spot 302 cubic inches (4.9 liters).
Equipped with an 11.0:1 compression ratio, solid lifters, aluminum intake, and an 800-cfm Holley four-barrel carburetor, the 302 V8 carried a rating of 290 hp (294 PS) at 5,800 rpm and 290 lb-ft (393 Nm) of torque at 4,200 rpm, while real output neared 360 hp (365 PS). Stock Muncie M21 4-speed cars reached 60 mph in 6.7 seconds and ran 14.9-second, 97-mph quarter-mile passes.
Photo: Facebook/Ryan Snyder When new, a 1967 Camaro Sport Coupe carried a base price of $2,466 in 6-cylinder trim or $2,572 in standard V8 form. Adding the $358.15 Z28 package, mandatory $100.10 power front disc brakes, heavy-duty F41 suspension, and the $184.35 Muncie 4-speed manual gearbox brought base Z/28 pricing to $3,215. Unbadged and barely promoted in 1967, Z/28 sales totaled 602 cars before surging to 7,199 in 1968 and 20,302 in 1969.
One of those 602 inaugural Z/28 coupes arrived at Fred Gibb Chevrolet in La Harpe, Illinois, on June 27, 1967, entering dealership inventory as a Demo 302 Camaro Racer. Gibb and his star salesman, drag racer Herb Fox, christened the Royal Plum coupe “Little Hoss” after Dan Blocker's Bonanza television character Hoss Cartwright and the small-displacement 302 V8. Raced initially with a cowl-plenum intake, Little Hoss went undefeated throughout 1967, with a track record (pun intentional) of 35-0.
In September 1967, Little Hoss claimed its first American Hot Rod Association world record just as East St. Louis tuning wizard Dick Harrell partnered with Fred Gibb. Harrell fortified the 302 V8 with forged JE pistons, a Howard's solid-lifter camshaft, Hooker headers, a Hays clutch, and a Lakewood scattershield. That combination propelled Little Hoss to an all-time best quarter-mile Elapsed Time of 11.75 seconds at 118.42 mph.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy After setting a 7.85-second 1/8-mile record at Beardstown Dragstrip on October 22, 1967, the team resprayed the exterior Cardinal Red for 1968 to match Harrell's Funny Cars, leaving the door jambs and underside of the trunk lid in factory Royal Plum. Fitted with Corvette knock-off wheels, a rear spoiler, and a cross-ram dual-quad intake shipped by Vince Piggins, Little Hoss captured the 1968 American Hot Rod Association Top Stock championship.
Winning Top Stock Eliminator at the August 1968 World Series of Drag Racing in Cordova, Illinois, plus Top Chevrolet Points Leader honors, convinced Fred Gibb to pursue even wilder factory race cars. As Ryan Snyder told Jim Campisano, it was this very 1967 Camaro Z/28 Little Hoss that directly sparked the fuse and inspired Gibb to order the first 50 examples of the fabled COPO Camaro with the all-aluminum ZL1 427-cubic-inch engines.
Gibb expected a price increase of about 400 bucks. He was off by one zero: the shocking $4,160.15 surcharge forced Chevrolet to redistribute most of them, as not many car nuts hoarded ZL1s from dealerships. As far as chevy performance went, only Baldwin-Motion could brag with a higher sticker price for Camaros, but those weren’t factory made racers like the ZL1s.
Photo: Mecum As for the Z/28 moniker, it went to become a legend, capturing back-to-back titles in 1968 and 1969 on the road racing circuits of Trans Am. However, as Little Hoss proved it in full, the car was more than capable of going very fast and very quick in short bursts of straight-line acceleration. Preserved with its original doors, trunk lid, and a New Old Stock 1967 CE-coded 302 short block, Little Hoss crossed the block in its red 1968 livery twice at Mecum Auctions, selling for $200,000 in Indianapolis in May 2022 and $195,000 in Kissimmee in January 2023.
Following that last sale, the historic Z/28 was stripped of Herb Fox's red respray and refinished in its original Royal Plum metallic racing glory, just like Fred Gibb had originally launched it into legendhood.

Covenant Logistics Group CEO David Parker expects truckload contract rates to increase by double digits in 2027 as trucking companies contend with rising operating expenses, tightening driver capacity and continued federal enforcement of safety regulations .
Speaking during the Chattanooga, Tennessee-based carrier’s third-quarter earnings call with analysts Friday, Parker said carriers will need additional rate increases to offset inflation in driver compensation, equipment, insurance and other operating costs .
“We’re going to continue to raise rates,” Parker said during the call. “We have to because of the cost.”
When an analyst asked whether the company expected another year of double-digit contract rate increases in 2027, Parker replied, “That’s my expectations.”
As of Thursday, shippers who reset their truckload contracts in recent months are paying about 12.8% more than the rates they replaced, according to SONAR’s Contract Rate Change Direction index (CRCD.USA). The rate is up from 4.1% during the same period in 2025.
The Contract Rate Change Direction index for the United States (CRCD.USA) measures the average percentage difference between a new contract base rate and the one it replaced within an established shipper-carrier relationship. It counts a change only when the old rate had held steady for more than 90 days. To learn more about SONAR, clic k here .
Covenant Logistics Group’s (NYSE: CVLG ) third-quarter results showed total revenue increasing 19.2% year over year to $353.9 million, while adjusted earnings per share rose to 50 cents from 44 cents a year earlier.
One of the most significant developments discussed during Friday’s call was Covenant’s transition away from traditional one-way expedited trucking toward multiyear committed capacity agreements.
Parker said approximately 25% of the company’s expedited trucks were operating under dedicated arrangements at the beginning of 2026. He expects that percentage to reach approximately 75% to 80% by the end of the year.
At the end of September, approximately 58% of Covenant’s expedited tractors were operating under committed capacity agreements, compared with about 40% at the end of the second quarter.
Parker said growing demand for high-security transportation, including technology-related shipments and equipment associated with data centers, is helping drive the transition.
“Technology loads have just been exploding,” Parker said.
Some customers are signing contracts lasting two to four years, providing Covenant with more predictable revenue and greater protection against fluctuations in freight volumes, according to Parker.
Unlike traditional expedited trucking, which historically emphasized maximizing miles and equipment utilization, the new arrangements often compensate Covenant for maintaining secure capacity even when trucks are waiting for shipments.
Some specialized operations may run approximately 3,000 miles per week, compared with 5,000 miles per week in the company’s traditional expedited network.
Parker said certain dedicated expedited contracts could eventually see operating ratios in the 80s, although he emphasized that those margins would apply to individual operations rather than the entire expedited segment.
Covenant executives said demand for specialized freight services remains strong, but finding qualified team drivers is becoming increasingly difficult.
Management said recruiting and training drivers capable of handling high-security freight requires additional time and resources, limiting how quickly the company can expand its specialized operations.
Management emphasized that its ability to capitalize on the demand depends on successfully recruiting qualified drivers, repositioning equipment and maintaining customer service.
The transition has already created operational challenges.
During the third quarter, Covenant reported an 8.9% reduction in its average truckload tractor fleet, which fell to 2,186 units from 2,400 a year earlier.
Truckload freight revenue excluding fuel surcharges declined 3.4% to $166 million, even as average freight revenue per total mile increased 19.8% to $3.03.
Covenant’s managed freight segment remained a major contributor to third-quarter earnings.
Managed freight revenue increased 68.4% to $121.6 million from $72.2 million a year earlier, while adjusted segment operating income rose approximately 133% to $7.1 million.
Management attributed the improvement to brokerage operations acquired during the fourth quarter of 2025, higher customer rates and improved availability of third-party carrier capacity.
Executives said the brokerage market experienced significant margin compression during the second quarter as spot freight rates increased rapidly.
However, conditions improved during the third quarter as purchased transportation costs eased while previously negotiated customer rate increases remained in place.
Management cautioned that the unusually strong third-quarter brokerage margins may not be sustainable every quarter.
Parker addressed the impact of federal trucking regulations on driver availability and freight capacity.
Responding to questions from analysts, Parker said he believes the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration remains committed to enforcement involving driver training schools, commercial driver’s licenses and electronic logging devices.
He said he had spoken with FMCSA officials the previous day and did not believe the agency was retreating from its enforcement priorities.
“We have been working closely with FMCSA, and we think they’re doing a great job,” Parker said.
Parker predicted that regulators would eventually require third-party certification of ELD providers as part of efforts to address falsified driver hours-of-service records.
He also said 30% of trucks using ELDs may be operating with manipulated records.
“I think it’s a gigantic number,” Parker said.
Parker said he expects continued enforcement to remove additional trucking capacity from the market, particularly in team-driver operations.
Looking beyond the fourth quarter, Covenant executives said the company’s long-term strategy will continue emphasizing specialized transportation, dedicated freight, brokerage and warehousing.
President Paul Bunn said the carrier intends to avoid pursuing low- margin , commoditized freight and instead focus on customers willing to support acceptable returns on invested capital.
“Number one, we’re going to be focused on safety and execution and not chasing stuff,” Bunn said.
The company also expects continued organic growth in its managed freight and warehousing segments, while remaining open to acquisitions and share repurchases depending on market conditions.
Covenant ended the third quarter with approximately $283.9 million in net indebtedness and an adjusted leverage ratio of about 2.1 times.
Management said it expects leverage to improve over the coming quarters as the company generates additional cash flow.
For the fourth quarter, Covenant anticipates a modest sequential increase in adjusted earnings per share, supported by improving truckload margins, partially offset by a smaller contribution from its 49% investment in transport enterprise leasing.
Longer term, executives said the combination of higher freight rates, more specialized contracts and reduced exposure to traditional over-the-road operations should strengthen the company’s profitability.

Toyota introduced a new family of lifted, “adventure-ready” Woodland concepts based on the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, Crown Signia, and bZ electric SUV.
Toyota expands the Woodland badge to new models
Toyota is the latest automaker to chase the highly profitable off-road market in the US, with plans to expand its “Woodland” lineup.
Although it already sells Woodland versions of the RAV4, Sienna, bZ, and most recently, the Grand Highlander, Toyota said the new family of concept vehicles is “designed for drivers who see adventure not as a destination, but a way of life.”
Toyota’s North American design studio, CALTY Design Research, designed the concepts to explore how some of its most popular nameplates can be used better on and off the road.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Each vehicle features Horizon Blue exterior paint, inspired by Toyota’s 1960s models, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona.
All new concepts also include an exclusive Woodland badge, plus a lift kit, large over-fenders, satin-black wheels, All-Terrain tires, two-tone paint on the roof and hood, a roof rack, and cross bars to top it off.
Toyota new Woodland concepts (Source: Toyota)
According to Toyota, the RAV4 Woodland Plug-In Hybrid and Sienna Woodland Concepts show how its “electrified and family-focused vehicles take on a more adventurous role.”
The electric Woodland bZ Concept “extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery electric future.” Meanwhile, the Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct models to the lineup, Toyota said.
The company didn’t reveal any powertrain specs or other details, but said the concepts show how capability can take many forms, including PHEV, hybrid, and battery electric.
Toyota’s new Woodland Concepts will be on display at the 2026 SEMA Show, starting on November 3.
To give you an idea, the 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower. That’s an extra 37 hp compared to the standard bZ with AWD.

Tesla has launched a new referral program in the US that pays owners in Full Self-Driving (Supervised) instead of rewarding car sales. A referred owner gets one free month of FSD, and the referrer gets a free month or a $99 Tesla Credit if that person starts paying.
At the same time, Tesla’s Refer and Earn terms no longer list any vehicle as a qualifying purchase for buyer or referrer rewards. Buy a Tesla with a friend’s code today and neither of you gets anything.
How the FSD referral works
To share a link, you need to be paying for FSD (Supervised) monthly or own it outright from before Tesla stopped selling it, according to Tesla’s FSD referral support page . Owners who got FSD through a one-year grant can’t participate. The link lives under “Refer and Earn” in the Tesla app, version 4.62.0 or later.
The person on the other end has to own a registered Tesla with compatible hardware, can’t have paid for FSD in the past 12 months, and can’t have bought it outright. There’s also a catch for recent buyers: anyone who got a free FSD trial with a new car is locked out of referral links until 12 months after that trial ends.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
If the friend converts, subscribers get a free month and outright owners get a $99 credit, the same as one month of the subscription. Credits expire after 12 months and can’t be cashed out. Tesla caps it at 12 rewards per calendar year, so the most anyone can earn is a year of FSD or $1,188 in credits.
Tesla’s own pages don’t quite agree on timing. The FSD page says the referrer is rewarded when the friend subscribes during the trial, while the main Refer and Earn page says after it.
Cars are out
The bigger change is buried in Tesla’s Refer and Earn page . Buyer benefits now apply to solar panels only. Referrer benefits cover solar, first demo drives (up to 30 over an account’s lifetime) and the new FSD referral.
Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck only show up under loyalty benefits, for existing owners buying another Tesla product. Model S and Model X aren’t listed at all.
Tesla didn’t announce the change. The page is stamped “Updated February 24, 2026,” so it’s unclear exactly when vehicles came off the list.
That’s quite a turn for a program that was always about moving cars. When Tesla brought the referral program back in August 2024 , a buyer got $1,000 off a Model S, X, Y or 3, and the referrer got $500 in credit. Tesla has killed and revived the program several times over the past decade, but cars were always at the center of it. Not anymore.
The metric that matters
Tesla stopped selling FSD outright on February 14, and new US customers can now only subscribe at $99 a month. In its Q3 shareholder letter, Tesla reported 1.74 million active FSD subscriptions , up 67% year-over-year, a count that includes past upfront buyers and excludes free trials.
That’s the exact metric in Elon Musk’s 2025 CEO Performance Award, which includes a milestone of 10 million active FSD subscriptions. It’s the reason Tesla started disclosing the number in January in the first place.
The free month a friend receives doesn’t count toward that total. A paid conversion does, and that’s precisely the event the new program pays for.
Electrek’s Take
This is a cheap program for Tesla and one directly built on what’s arguably now its main business: selling FSD. Tesla used to hand out $1,000 discounts to drive referrals. Now it gives away a month of software that’s already sitting in the car, and the referrer gets either more of that same software or a credit that can only be spent at Tesla. In exchange, Tesla gets a $99-a-month subscriber.
The recipient has to already own a Tesla, so the program doesn’t add a single car to the fleet. It’s built to mine the existing fleet for subscriptions. Tesla had sold about 8.9 million vehicles by the end of 2025, and only 1.74 million are paying for FSD, so there’s plenty of room. At Q3’s pace, we estimated 10 million subscriptions is still about eight years away.
So Tesla stopped paying for referrals that require selling a car, and started paying for the ones that move the number in Musk’s pay package. We think that tells you a lot about where the company’s priorities are right now.

WASHINGTON — On the Pentagon’s long journey towards the real-time sharing of data between allies, a key official said 2026 marked the year in which partners in the Pacific, at least, were able to see the battlefield with a common operational picture (COP) and act as one.
“This was really the first year that all of our capabilities are in a multilateral environment where our partners are using those warfighting applications and tools with the US and we have a single COP to conduct warfighting,” Brig. Gen. Michael Smith, director for command, control, communications, computers and cyber at Indo-Pacific Command said Thursday at the TechNet Indo-Pacific Conference.
Smith was referencing what he and other officials called the PACOM Mission Network, a system that allows US forces and partners to share data and mission planning tools securely, across classification to jointly conduct operations or prosecute targets.
US officials for years have discussed the notion and need for so-called mission partner networks or environments to enable multiple nations to plan together. That effort, like other pieces of the even larger Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control initiative, is made difficult by different data sources, standards and classification.
But officials noted those challenges are being overcome in the Pacific.
“What’s the so what? So what is our partners are now doing warfighting functions in our mission partner environment,” Smith said. “We’ve had a lot of legacy bilat[eral] systems and networks. Some of those still exist, but now we have a common operational environment that’s multilateral, data-centric, zero trust -enabled. … And the partners are really excited about that.”
The system was used during “several major exercises” over the last year, Lt. Gen. George Rowell, PACOM’s deputy commander, said Thursday at the conference. While he didn’t specify how many exercises it participated in, he noted the command conducted 17 exercises across nine host nations and incorporating 35 countries.
“For the first time, PACOM and several key allies and partners communicated, collaborated, planned, and executed with common tools, common data flows and language translation,” he said. “The real story of these exercises was more than the missiles on the rails. It was our ability to pass that sensor-to-shooter targeting information, data, and the evolving science of the pipes connecting everything across that vast tyranny of distance.”
Smith provided one example in which for the first time Japanese partners used the Maven Smart System, an artificial intelligence-enabled platform used for planning and targeting, which is embedded into the mission network. Using Maven, Japanese are contributing to joint strikes and close kill chains, he said.
Rowell equated these collaboration abilities to deterrence.
“This deterrent capability becomes credible when we prove to any potential adversary that our commanders can execute without missing a beat, even when primary systems are jammed or disabled,” he said. “Assured command and control is inseparable from the concept of deterrence here in the Pacific.”

Alain Bedard, the CEO of TFI International, had been highly critical of his company’s U.S. LTL operations back in 2024, at one point referring to some of its practices as “stupid.”
As recently as April, he was far more optimistic about the segment that was built largely through the TFI acquisition of UPS Freight in 2021.
But on Friday, after a third quarter earnings report that had the performance of TFI’s LTL operations lagging well behind its Truckload segment, and with Wall Street punishing the stock almost as soon as the earnings were released late Thursday, Bedard on the company’s earnings call didn’t hold back in a candor that would be shocking in similar forums in almost any industry.
“Truckload is great,” Bedard said, discussing the quarter. “Logistics is great. U.S. LTL is not and I feel like I’m a broken record on that. We’ve got to correct the situation.”
New leader coming in
Bedard said a new manager of the U.S. LTL operations is being brought in by TFI (NYSE: TFII) though he would not disclose the person’s identity. “We need management to jump in and do the right thing,” he said.
Bedard referred to the U.S. LTL operations at TFI as “a rock in my shoe.”
At approximately 2:15 EDT, TFI stock was down 14.71%, or $16.55, to $95.99. Even with that decline, it is still up 11.24% for the last 52 weeks. It is also solidly above the 52-week low of $80.63, recorded almost a year ago on November 20.
While TFI does not break out an OR for U.S. and Canada separately, the company-wide OR for LTL in the third quarter was 91.3% compared to 88.8% a year earlier.
U.S. LTL OR pushing 100
But Bedard offered specifics during the call. “When we report a 91 OR, you can think that our U.S. operation is closer to a 97 and our Canadian operation is more like a sub 75,” he said. But he said Canadian shipments are about 10,000 per day, compared to about 20,000 in the U.S.
Bedard cited as a negative comparison the operating ratio at other LTL carriers without identifying them by name. But Old Dominion Freight Lines (NASDAQ: ODFL) reported a 71.5% OR for the quarter, while XPO (NYSE: XPO) was just over 80%.
Bedard took pains in the call to not attack the unions that represent the workers in its LTL operations, repeatedly saying that many of the group’s issues were with management.
But he also said in the U.S., “there’s nothing we can do except build some kind of non-union network in parallel to the network that we have.”
Hercules a key going forward
The key to that effort will be Hercules Forwarding, which TFI bought in 2024. Bedard said Hercules is a non-union operation that TFI now uses for about 1,000 LTL shipments per day.
“This is small,” he said.”But unless there is something of size that comes to us, the plan is going to be to slowly build that non-union company, like we do in Canada.”
Bedard said TFI’s Canadian LTL operations are both union and non-union, “so it’s OK. We’ll run a second network if we can.”
The goal, he said, “would be to bring more stability to TForce,” the name of the U.S. LTL operations.
In earlier criticisms of TForce operations, Bedard has focused on two key operational areas: density and weight. In both cases, Bedard’s complaint has been that there is too little of either.
Density was raised as an issue again by Bedard in the Friday call. One measure that illustrates the problem, according to Bedard: “the average mile that we drive today between each and every stop in our (U.S.) package and delivery operation is about twice as much as our Canadian operation.”
“In Canada, we focus on trying to do business with customers that are close by and not run 100 miles to do a delivery,” he said. TFI has been trying to change that sort of “culture” at US LTL, Bedard said, “but it seems difficult to do.”
The unidentified new hire “is hopefully going to be able to help us drive change.” But Bedard added that “there are more team members that we need to drive more change and to bring that density down.”
Density issues magnified by diesel
The issue of density in U.S. LTL has become an even larger issue at TFI because of fuel costs, Bedard said.
In response to an analyst question, Bedard said the new hire has been on the job since October 1. The executive’s identity will be revealed soon, with Bedard only saying the person had been retired from an industry peer.
“A new broom sweeps clean” he said. “We have got to change the recipe and that’s what we’re doing now.”
He said the U.S. LTL operations are beset by a “mentality of, we really don’t care.” Bedard said that was a legacy of the UPS (NYSE: UPS) ownership, which directed its interest and investment dollars to its more traditional business.
Not for sale
Bedard’s comments were stark enough that it led one analyst to ask a question that would have been unthinkable not all that long ago: might TFI divest its U.S. LTL operations?
Bedard gave a lengthy answer that eventually circled back to a “no.”
“If you look at TForce, we want to be in LTL,” he said. “So to me, it’s been a disappointment. I’m not happy with what’s going on, but it’s a fight. We’ve been fighting but losing.”
He wrapped up his response with a “no.”
“We have no intention of selling our US LTL operations at all,” Bedard said. “We want those guys to be efficient, to be productive and after improving everything except the human side of the business, it’s not working.”
The entire problem is “human,” he added. “There’s no more excuse on the fleet,” he said. “There’s no more excuse on the financial tools. It’s just that we have the wrong guys.”
Bedard did speak positively about the company’s Truckload operations, which recorded an OR of 86.7% for the quarter.
Positive words for Daseke
Part of the strength in Truckload is being driven by the operations that came with the purchase of flatbed operator Daseke in 2023 , which had been a publicly traded company.
As recently as the first quarter of last year, Bedard said on the company’s earnings call that the integration of Daseke had been a struggle.
But that was not the message he delivered this year. “Daseke has been turned around very, very fast,” he said. He cited OR performance before the purchase of 97-98%
A review of FreightWaves articles on Daseke earnings from the quarters immediately before the TFI acquisition mostly shows OR performance at either side of 90.
While Daseke is not the only asset in TFI’s Truckload segment, it helped the operations come in with an OR of 86.7% for the quarter.
“The Canadian operation is doing even better, but our U.S. operation is slowly catching up,” Bedard said.

MAILLY-LE-CAMP, France — Corporal Igor started a new job this year, swapping the sights of a 105 mm gun on the French Army’s AMX 10 RC reconnaissance vehicle for first-person view goggles and a handheld controller.
The 21-year-old is now a strike pilot in France’s first dedicated drone-combat squadron, crouching in nettles and tall grass as he guided an FPV drone down a forest path at the Mailly-le-Camp training area east of Paris during a June exercise of the 1st Marine Infantry Regiment, or 1er RIMa.
“We’re switching specialties, we’re keeping up with the times,” said the corporal, who last year still manned the gunner seat in the AMX 10 RC armored car.
Inspired by the war in Ukraine, the 1er RIMa converted one of its three light cavalry squadrons into an experimental all-drone unit, with results so convincing that the Army is rushing more drone formations into service. The aim is for around 15 drone-combat units by summer 2027 and more by the end of next year, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Jacques de Montgros said this month.
France deployed a drone-combat unit to Romania for the first time in recent weeks as part of Mission Aigle, the French-led mission to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank, and will deploy a second unit to Poland for an exercise next month, de Montgros told lawmakers in an Oct. 14 hearing. “So we’re really at a point of scaling up our efforts in these areas.”
Cpl. Igor of the French Army’s 1st Marine Infantry Regiment operates an FPV drone during a training exercise at Mailly-le-Camp on June 11, 2026. (Rudy Ruitenberg/staff)
The 1er RIMa’s experimental squadron has provided a blueprint to create more tactical drone formations, while offering the French Army a lesson in the vulnerability of NATO-style combined-arms tactics to drone threats. During exercises this year, the regiment’s pilots hunted armored vehicles and command posts of the opposing force, disrupting maneuver and force buildup.
Mixing surveillance drones, FPV one-way attack drones and loitering munitions, the 1er Escadron de Drones de Chasse, which roughly translates as 1st Hunter-Drone Squadron, has also been a test bed for the Army, partnering with French firms to work on swarming technology, autonomous terminal guidance and launch canisters.
France’s first drone squadron grew from an idea within the 1er RIMa’s training and operations office in late 2023, to develop a way of fighting with drones that went beyond just adding them to existing units. The concept built on a proposal by Capt. Guillaume, an open-source intelligence specialist who had been studying the war in Ukraine.
When the office tested an experimental drone unit in a tactical exercise, the drones created “a crazy amount of disruption,” said Col. Aymeric Caussin, commander of the 1er RIMa, who headed the office at the time. “So we said, right, let’s go for it.”
Cavalry heritage
Drawing on the regiment’s light cavalry heritage, the squadron was designed as a mobile force with drones as its weapons system, said Lt. Col Remi, who worked to implement the idea during a two-year stint in the 1er RIMa. Light cavalry principles still applied: gather intelligence, then fix, outflank and ultimately destroy the enemy, with a focus on mobility, dispersion and stealth.
“We needed a squadron that evoked the light cavalry: ‘drone’ because that’s its primary weapon system, and ‘hunter’ because that’s what we actually do in the field.”
The regiment tested the concept during Exercise Hedgehog in Estonia in May 2025, sending some 10 drone pilots as part of a French combined-arms tactical group. The U.S. 5th squadron, 7th Cavalry Regiment served as the designated opposing force during the exercise, with dismounted soldiers and M2A4 Bradley Fighting Vehicles.
The Wall Street Journal previously reported how Ukrainian operators taking part in the exercise exposed the vulnerability of NATO troops to drone warfare. The French team equally showed the impact of drones on an opponent unprepared for the threat.
The French pilots, who made up around 5% of the tactical group’s active strength, accounted for 20% of the attrition inflicted on the opposing force of American troops with Bradleys in a single day of combat, said Maj. Sylvain, head of operations at the 1er RIMa, who attended the exercise.
The virtual devastation convinced French Army leaders to scale up the experiment. Within two months, the drone squadron was made official, and in early April 2026 the Army staff declared it “ fully operational .”
“It was the proof of concept,” Maj. Sylvain said. “Everything falls into place, everyone is supportive of the project, and the regiment decides to transform the first squadron into a hunter-drone squadron.”
The drone team also brought several startups to Estonia for Hedgehog 25, including Alta Ares and Icarus Swarms, while Naval Group joined at its own expense. The 1er RIMa works with Alta Ares on AI-enabled detection and reconnaissance, Icarus Swarms on autonomous navigation and computer-assisted piloting, and Naval Group on drone-launch canisters.
The drone squadron has continue to rack up the virtual kills since Hedgehog. During France’s large-scale exercise Orion 2026, the 1er RIMa’s drone pilots tallied four regimental command posts, a number of logistics convoys and anti-drone and air-defense units, according to Caussin.
‘Quite a bit of damage’
What made the drone-combat unit stand out was its responsiveness, with FPV drones able to quickly close gaps in the lines and attack the main axis of enemy efforts, and its ability to disrupt the enemy command structures, particularly by directly targeting command posts, Caussin said.
“Through the drone, we’ll seek to disrupt the enemy’s chain of command. We’re influencing decision-making.”
Orion 2026 showed that distance no longer protects. The squadron’s intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance drones detected tactical command posts several kilometers from the front line, then called in artillery or directed FPV drones to attack, said Staff Sgt. Tristan, who leads a platoon of FPV pilots after about 12 years on the AMX 10 RC.
Troops of the French Army’s 1st Marine Infantry Regiment launch an FPV drone from a canister during an exercise at the Mailly-le-Camp training grounds on June 11, 2026. (Rudy Ruitenberg/staff)
The regiment inflicted “quite a bit of damage” with drones and artillery, “but had it been the other way around, it would have been the same,” Staff Sgt. Tristan said. “If we’d been facing a unit like ours and we would have stayed in the AMX 10 RC, well, we would’ve been wiped out a lot too, right? So you have to put things in perspective.”
During an exercise in March at Mailly-le-Camp, the 1er RIMa acted as the opposing force during the combat preparation of another French light-cavalry regiment. The drone squadron’s pilots attacked and virtually destroyed enemy armor, or would track vehicles to command posts or troop concentrations before striking, paralyzing enemy movement.
The result was “severe,” said FPV pilot Igor, who participated in the exercise. The opposing force was neutralized, at least virtually.
For the Army, the takeaway was that it wanted to equip five more regiments with an all-drone squadron, to be operational in 2027. With the Army accelerating its drone effort, the six combat-drone units will be operational by the year, said Gen. Bruno Baratz, head of Future Combat Command, at an innovation day organized by France’s 6th Armored Brigade in September.
The brigade, which was assigned to set up two of the five drone squadrons, decided to create a third drone-combat unit using its own resources, 6th Armored Brigade commander Gen. Maxime do Tran said at the innovation day. One of the brigade’s infantry regiments is now deployed to Romania with a drone-combat unit.
“The trial conducted by the 1st Marine Infantry Regiment demonstrated the value of this capability,” Do Tran said. “We didn’t wait.”
With the drone-combat squadron of the 1er RIMa “more of a cavalry, reconnaissance” unit, Do Tran says the 6th Armored Brigade has taken a slightly different approach for its infantry regiments, ensuring that drone pilots previously trained on the Akeron antitank missile or 81-millimeter mortars retain those skills through dual training.
He said the brigade staff realized that whenever the weather was unfavorable for drone operations, those dual capabilities were needed to retain lethality. Creating drone units also created a problem of mass, according to Do Tran.
During the brigade’s first combat-preparation exercises with combat-drones, commanders found that even if their drone pilots achieved initial saturation, a numerically strong enemy would still break through lines that lacked ground troops to stop a large force.
“We quickly get overwhelmed if we don’t also have men behind them with rifles or other weapons,” Do Tran said. “We need to maintain a certain balance between human mass and drone pilots.”
Combat-drone units will have different uses based on the regiment they’re part of, according to the general.
He said that for a light cavalry regiment such as the 1st RIMa, drones contribute to reconnaissance and intelligence gathering, while for an infantry regiment, the primary role will be delivering lethal firepower. For a regiment of Leclerc main battle tanks, the combat drone unit’s primary role is to protect the armored column, Do Tran said.
“ It’s an entirely new set of rules to learn, an entirely new combination of capabilities to reinvent,” said Baratz. “The Army’s task today is to reinvent itself to be effective in this modern combat.”
Drone vulnerabilities
“ We shouldn’t think that drones will make the old systems obsolete. Drones do have vulnerabilities: weather conditions, electronic jamming, other counter-drone systems being put in place. We still need our older systems for deep-strike operations, close-contact maneuvers and direct engagement.”
Officers of the 1er RIMa cautioned against over-interpreting the March exercise, with Maj. Sylvain saying the opposing regiment lacked adequate anti-drone capabilities and had few drones of its own, making an effective response difficult. Caussin likewise noted that during Orion, the exercise in free terrain limited realistic use of jamming by the opposing force.
Equipment used by the French Army’s 1st Marine Infantry Regiment is on display during an exercise at the Mailly-le-Camp training grounds on June 11, 2026. (Rudy Ruitenberg/staff)
“If we’re back in a tank tomorrow and opposite of us we have another drone unit, it’s going to be tough for us as well,” Staff Sgt. Tristan said. “So we need all this feedback to figure out how to fight back against that.”
For its own combat preparation in June, the 1er RIMa asked the Centac combined-arms training center that runs the exercises at Mailly-le-Camp to step up the challenge, particularly by creating a contested electronic warfare environment.
The training center also added 12-gauge shotguns to the infantry kit and emphasized camouflage. Soldiers unfolded camouflaged umbrellas bought at sporting goods store Decathlon whenever they were on the move, seeking to obscure their visual signature.
The umbrellas slowed the 1er RIMa’s drone operators, forcing them to spend more time identifying targets to avoid confusion with the numerous deer or boars at Mailly-le-Camp, said Lt. Col. Guillaume, head of training at the 1st Light Infantry Battalion that staffs the center.
The opposing force also remained more dispersed, avoided grouped movement and kept vehicles farther back, bringing them forward only when the situation was considered sufficiently safe. The transparency provided by drones clearly changed how the exercise unfolded and affected the conduct of operations, Lt. Col. Guillaume said.
While the drone advantage was less pronounced in June than in March, the 1er RIMa’s drone squadron obtained the best score of the roughly 30 Army units that passed through the Mailly-le-Camp training center over a 12-month period, Lt. Col. Guillaume said. The June exercise provided a better assessment of how the drone squadron fares against a more capable adversary, according to Caussin.
The regiment explored what might happen if the tactical deadlock observed in Ukraine were broken and maneuver is restored, with Caussin saying the drone squadron’s mobility would allow it to move rapidly between different parts of the battlefield, using drones to understand the tactical situation and fill gaps.
But the exercise also showed the battlefield overview provided by drones, while necessary to win an engagement, is not enough by itself. The speed at which intelligence can be converted into action is as important as the number of drones in the air, and traditional infantry elements remained necessary to provide direct kinetic action, Lt. Col. Guillaume said.
Jam detection
Electronic warfare reduced drone effectiveness on several occasions, allowing the opposing force to bring in armor to create a temporary advantage and secure objectives, said Lt. Col. Guillaume, describing a constant “game of cat and mouse.”
Because of the energy requirements of electronic warfare, jamming is not necessarily continuous. The regiment learned it needed to become better at determining when it was actually being jammed by the adversary, and when a failed maneuver was due to its own poor execution, according to Caussin.
For the regimental commander, the exercise confirmed the drone squadron complements rather than replaces armored formations, an additional layer to combined-arms warfare than a revolution. With the opponent better prepared for the drone threat, the June exercise forced the 1er RIMa to change how it employed drones, picking priority targets rather than observing and striking at will.
In a drone-saturated environment, advantage will come more from controlling the pace of events rather than simply holding ground, by combining drones and highly mobile forces to observe, adapt, and act faster than the adversary, according to Caussin.
He called the stand-out quality of the drone-combat unit its ability “manipulate the enemy’s decision-making time, really to overwhelm them” and allow the regiment to seize the initiative.
“Will the drone’s enemy be another drone?” Caussin said. “We’re starting to implement this to some extend in small-scale exercises, particularly at the regimental level.”
“It’s always difficult to talk about game-changers. What’s certain today is that this is the reality of the battlefield and it enables us to achieve tactical effects that have a decisive impact on the enemy.”
In the 1er RIMa, FVP pilots are teamed with a driver, a vehicle commander and optionally a fourth crew member operating a drone by Paris-based vendor Parrot, or other ISR system to designate targets. Cpl. Igor said he often works with one crew member as a spotter. The teams still carry Heckler & Koch rifles, a heavy machine gun to defend against enemy infantry, and an AT4 shoulder-fired antitank weapon.
Farther reach
With the 105 mm gun of the AMX 10 RC, “we had reach, but we were much more visible,” Staff Sgt. Tristan said. Now, “we hole up in a corner with our vehicle and launch our drones from hiding, so the enemy can’t see us. With an AMX 10 RC, we can’t do that.”
The regiment’s drone squadron retained the structure of an armored reconnaissance unit, with a command and logistics platoon and four combat platoons: an ISR unit, two FPV drone units and one platoon operating longer-range loitering munitions.
With around 100 drone pilots in a unit of 120 personnel, the squadron can provide intelligence and strike across an area typically covered by a formation several times larger, with an operational reach approaching that of a full combined-arms tactical group, according to Lt. Col. Remi.
A team from the French Army’s 1st Marine Infantry Regiment operates an FPV drone during an exercise at the Mailly-le-Camp training grounds on June 11, 2026. (Rudy Ruitenberg/staff)
The large number of drone operators changes logistics. Supply vehicles carry drones rather than ammunition, and the unit needs battlefield energy generation to keep batteries topped up. FPV pilot Igor said that during a day of exercise and simulated strikes, he might go through 10 or 20 drones.
Both Caussin and Maj. Sylvain emphasized drones alone will not decide a battle. The squadron is designed to operate alongside conventional units and slot into larger formations, with interoperability with French Army units and NATO allies built in from the start, said Maj. Sylvain.
In addition to developing doctrine, the regiment’s mandate is to work with industrial partners on technologies to make the drone squadron more effective. Once concept, described by officers and pilots as “queen and workers,” involves an operator controlling a mother drone, or queen, which in turn steers multiple worker drones launched from a “hive,” or canister.
The goal is essentially fire-and-forget autonomous engagement, according to Maj. Sylvain. An operator assigns a mission, the queen autonomously seeks and identifies the designated target, then directs worker drones to destroy it without further operator intervention.
With the squadron conceived as a mobile force rather than one dug in like Ukrainian operators, the idea is to have four hives at the back of a vehicle, with a stock of drones ready to deploy, Staff Sgt. Tristan said.
“Just open the hives, send out four drones on autopilot, and let them carry out their mission.”
While “not everything works perfect,” the squadron and its industry partners have figured out queen-worker communications and terminal guidance, Maj. Sylvain said.
FPV drone hit rates might be 5% to 10% for a novice pilot and 30% for an experienced one, compared with a more than 90% chance to land a shot with the AMX 10 RC cannon, according to Staff Sgt. Tristan. The regiment is counting on autonomous terminal guidance to increase drone hit rates to around 80% to 90%.
The squadron’s doctrinal goals include FPV strikes at a distance of 10 kilometers, and communication range is the main practical obstacle, Maj. Sylvain said. The ISR platoon uses several drone models from Parrot and is starting to achieve the ranges of up to 20 kilometers called for in the doctrine.
Officers in the 1er RIMa shied away from comparisons with Ukrainian drone units, which Maj. Sylvain said are battle-hardened after several years of war.
‘We’re not naive’
“It’s obvious that we’d learn a lot from an exercise against them,” he said. “We’re not naive. We’re fully aware of our current level of capability, and we know we still have a lot of work to do to be ready to deploy the drone-combat squadron in a high-intensity conflict.”
The June exercise was also an opportunity to work on defense against enemy UAVs.
“Camouflage ourselves, take cover, and make sure there’s always someone listening out for drones, either to destroy them with certain weapons or simply to hide,” Staff Sgt. Tristan said. “In the heat of battle, chasing down a vehicle, also staying alert for anti-drone is difficult.”
The constant drone threat changes daily life for soldiers on exercise. Rather than having fixed meal times, “you have to snack throughout the day,” said Staff Sgt. Tristan. Sleep also becomes fragmented, with drone surveillance continuing through the night.
The 1er RIMa itself has adapted its command structure to the drone presence, dividing up command posts and deploying in the same armored vehicles as combat units to avoid detection.
“We question ourselves, we wonder how we can protect ourselves from this too,” said Cpl. Igor, the FPV pilot. “If we’re capable of doing it, we’re not the only ones who know how. So we’re going to try to find ways to protect ourselves from drones, because they’re really effective.”
